ety.text: From Middle English geaunt, geant, from Old French geant, gaiant (Modern French géant) from Vulgar Latin *gagās, gagant-, from Latin gigās, gigant-, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”). Cognate to giga- (“1,000,000,000”). Largely Displaced native Old English ent (“giant”), Old English eoten (“giant or jötunn”), and Old English þyrs (“giant or ogre”). Compare English ent (“giant tree-man”), ettin (“giant or troll”) and thurse (“giant”).

senses.d: A mythical human or humanoid of very great size.
Any of the gigantes, the race of giants in the Greek mythology.

ex: The giants also had been outlawed along with Satan because they had fought against god.

senses.d: A very tall and large person.
ex: "It's barbarous, Norsus." "It's Rome," said the giant flatly.

senses.d: A tall species of a particular animal or plant.
A star that is considerably more luminous than a main sequence star of the same temperature.
An Ethernet packet that exceeds the medium's maximum packet size of 1,518 bytes.

ex: The retail giant is set to acquire two more struggling high-street chains.
Swiss food giant Nestlé confirmed the theft, which disappeared while traveling from central Italy to Poland.

senses.d: A person of extraordinary strength or powers, bodily or intellectual.
A maneuver involving a full rotation around an axis while fully extended.
